question_text: In the context of this course, the phrase "digital signal processing" is best understood as:
options: The branch of electronics devoted to designing analog amplifiers and filters
The study of how physical sensors convert measured quantities into voltages
The theories, methods and algorithms for processing signals in digital form
The fabrication of microprocessor chips from raw semiconductor wafer material
correct_answer: The theories, methods and algorithms for processing signals in digital form

question_text: The term "digital signal processor" (as opposed to "digital signal processing") refers to:
options: A kind of microprocessor used to implement digital signal processing algorithms
The mathematical algorithm through which an input signal is passed for its result
The analog front-end that band-limits a signal before it reaches the converter
The high-level software language in which the processing routines are written
correct_answer: A kind of microprocessor used to implement digital signal processing algorithms

question_text: An analog signal is best characterised as one that is:
options: Continuous in both time and magnitude
Continuous in time but discrete in magnitude
Discrete in time but continuous in magnitude
Discrete in both time and magnitude
correct_answer: Continuous in both time and magnitude

question_text: A digital signal is best characterised as one that is:
options: Discrete in both time and magnitude
Continuous in both time and magnitude
Continuous in time but discrete in magnitude
Discrete in time but continuous in magnitude
correct_answer: Discrete in both time and magnitude

question_text: Before a real-world analog signal can be processed digitally, two transformations must be applied in order. They are:
options: Quantize the signal in amplitude first, then sample it at discrete time points
Sample the signal at discrete time points, then quantize the sample values
Amplify the signal to full scale, then shift its frequency into a lower band
Filter the signal to remove noise, then store it directly in continuous form
correct_answer: Sample the signal at discrete time points, then quantize the sample values

question_text: Quantization of a sampled signal is normally carried out by:
options: Delaying each sample value by one sampling interval before it is stored
Averaging each sample value together with its two nearest neighbours
Rounding or truncating each sample value to an available level
Multiplying each sample value by a fixed scaling constant before storage
correct_answer: Rounding or truncating each sample value to an available level

question_text: Why must most real-world signals be transformed before a DSP system can operate on them?
options: Most real-world signals are already digital and merely need to be amplified
Most real-world signals are analog, while DSP works on signals in digital form
DSP systems can handle periodic signals but reject aperiodic ones outright
DSP systems require a signal to be expressed in the frequency domain first
correct_answer: Most real-world signals are analog, while DSP works on signals in digital form

question_text: Which statement best captures the relationship between digitization and DSP that the course uses to motivate the subject?
options: Digitization and DSP are competing techniques for handling the same signals
DSP is a narrow niche that has little bearing on the modern information technology field
Digitization underpins information technology, and its kernel is digital signal processing
Digitization replaced DSP once integrated circuits became widely available
correct_answer: Digitization underpins information technology, and its kernel is digital signal processing

question_text: A key reason a digital system offers greater programmability than an analog system is that:
options: A digital system needs no software at all once its hardware has been fixed
A digital system rewires its own internal circuits as its requirements change
An analog system is reconfigured purely by editing its onboard firmware code
A digital system can be changed by modifying software rather than hardware
correct_answer: A digital system can be changed by modifying software rather than hardware

question_text: An engineer swaps a standard filter for an adaptive filter simply by loading new code, leaving the hardware untouched. This illustrates which advantage of digital systems?
options: Programmability
Anti-noise performance
Large-scale integration
Real-time response
correct_answer: Programmability

question_text: In a digital system, the precision of the processing is chiefly governed by:
options: The tolerance ratings printed on the resistors and the capacitors used
The number of ADC bits, the processor word-length and the algorithm used
The ambient temperature and the humidity of the operating environment
The physical length of the wiring that connects the components together
correct_answer: The number of ADC bits, the processor word-length and the algorithm used

question_text: Why is an analog system's precision considered harder to guarantee than a digital system's?
options: Analog precision depends on component tolerances, such as resistors within 5% or capacitors within 20%
Analog precision is fixed by the bit count of its analog-to-digital converter alone
Analog components retain their exact printed rated values throughout their whole service life
Analog systems round each sample coarsely, discarding the finer detail of the signal
correct_answer: Analog precision depends on component tolerances, such as resistors within 5% or capacitors within 20%

question_text: With respect to stability, how does a digital system typically compare with an analog one as temperature and humidity vary?
options: The digital system drifts more because its logic gates are temperature-sensitive
The digital system shows essentially no variation across its rated operating range
Both systems drift by roughly the same amount for a given change in temperature
The digital system grows unstable while the analog system holds its values steady
correct_answer: The digital system shows essentially no variation across its rated operating range

question_text: The characteristics of analog components such as resistors, capacitors and op-amps are a concern for stability because they:
options: Change with temperature, humidity and similar environmental conditions
Grow hard to measure accurately once they are soldered onto a circuit board
Consume far more electrical power than the equivalent digital logic gates do
Can be readjusted afterwards by rewriting the controlling software routines
correct_answer: Change with temperature, humidity and similar environmental conditions

question_text: The repeatability advantage of digital systems refers to the property that:
options: A single digital unit can process many different inputs at the same time
A digital signal can be repeated indefinitely without needing any storage
Digital units detect and correct a wrong result soon after producing it
Identical digital units process the same input into the same output
correct_answer: Identical digital units process the same input into the same output

question_text: Error-correcting codes are cited as an advantage of digital representation because they:
options: Compress the data so that fewer bits need to be sent over the channel
Scramble the data so that unauthorised receivers are unable to read it
Convert the data back into an analog form that is suited to transmission
Add redundant bits so that introduced errors can be detected and corrected
correct_answer: Add redundant bits so that introduced errors can be detected and corrected

question_text: Regarding fidelity in storage and transmission, the slides argue that:
options: The fidelity of the analog medium exceeds that of the digital medium
Digital and analog media deliver essentially identical fidelity in practice
The fidelity of the digital medium is greater than that of the analog medium
Fidelity is governed mainly by the length of the transmission cable used
correct_answer: The fidelity of the digital medium is greater than that of the analog medium

question_text: How does the course contrast analog and digital data compression?
options: Analog compression is the genuinely lossless kind, whereas digital compression loses information
Neither analog nor digital compression is able to preserve the full information
Analog compression loses some information, whereas digital technology makes lossless compression possible
Digital compression suits images well but is not applicable to audio signals
correct_answer: Analog compression loses some information, whereas digital technology makes lossless compression possible

question_text: The 3 kHz bandwidth limit applied to analog telephone lines is given as an example of:
options: A lossless digital compression scheme applied to the line
An error-correcting code operating on the telephone line
Analog compression in which some information is lost
A sampling operation carried out before the quantization step
correct_answer: Analog compression in which some information is lost

question_text: Which is listed as a genuine limitation of digital signal processing rather than an advantage?
options: Digital systems drift heavily whenever the operating temperature changes
A/D and D/A conversion rates are not available for some applications, such as beyond GHz
Digital systems resist any reprogramming once they have been deployed out in the field
Digital systems are unable to store their data for later retrieval and use
correct_answer: A/D and D/A conversion rates are not available for some applications, such as beyond GHz

question_text: One reason analog processing is still needed is real-time performance, because in an analog system:
options: The processing time is set by the processor speed and the chosen algorithm
Aside from circuit delay, the processing happens in real time
The signal must first be sampled before any output can begin to appear
Each result must wait for a redundant error-correction pass to finish first
correct_answer: Aside from circuit delay, the processing happens in real time

question_text: Why can analog systems still be preferred for very high-frequency signals such as microwave or light-wave signals?
options: Analog systems can store such high-frequency signals far more compactly than digital ones
Such signals are limited by sample-and-hold, ADC and processor speeds, and fast ADCs cost a lot
Very high-frequency signals carry no useful information that is worth the effort of digitizing
Digital systems are designed to reject any signal lying above the standard audio band by rule
correct_answer: Such signals are limited by sample-and-hold, ADC and processor speeds, and fast ADCs cost a lot

question_text: The remark that "most signals in the real world are analog" is used in the course to argue that:
options: Analog signals are best kept in analog form rather than converted into digital form
DSP systems have by now made analog processing very nearly obsolete in practice
Real-world signals arrive already sampled by nature and so need no conversion step
Mixed-signal processing is needed to convert such signals into digital form for a DSP system
correct_answer: Mixed-signal processing is needed to convert such signals into digital form for a DSP system

question_text: Base stations, switching centres and mobile phones are given as DSP applications under which broad area?
options: Medical imaging
Satellite navigation
Consumer photography
Communications
correct_answer: Communications

question_text: GPS and GIS are cited as DSP applications belonging to which area?
options: Measurement and control
Satellite navigation
Military and safety
Consumer electronics
correct_answer: Satellite navigation

question_text: Ultrasound, MRI and CT scanning are used in the slides as DSP examples in the field of:
options: Medical imaging and analysis
Industrial measurement and control
Wireless communication systems
Satellite navigation and timing
correct_answer: Medical imaging and analysis

question_text: MP3 audio decoding, digital cameras and HDTV are grouped in the slides under which application area?
options: Military and safety
Consumer electronics
Biomedical analysis
Industrial control
correct_answer: Consumer electronics

question_text: The general problem of signal analysis and processing is framed in the course as:
options: Letting signals pass through systems and studying the response
Storing signals in memory and later retrieving them unchanged
Converting each signal into one single fixed reference frequency
Stripping the timing information from a signal before it is used
correct_answer: Letting signals pass through systems and studying the response

question_text: The general strategy the course recommends for analysing a complicated signal through a system is to:
options: Represent the signal as a sum of simple signals, get each response, then add the responses
Measure the output for the whole complicated signal without first decomposing it
Replace the whole system with a single resistor-and-capacitor network before analysing
Convert the input into one constant value before it is applied to the system
correct_answer: Represent the signal as a sum of simple signals, get each response, then add the responses

question_text: A signal f(t) for which f(t) = 0 for all t < 0 is called:
options: A periodic signal
A causal signal
An even signal
A singularity signal
correct_answer: A causal signal

question_text: Multiplying an arbitrary (possibly non-causal) signal by the unit step u(t) has the effect of:
options: Turning it into a causal signal that is zero for t < 0
Shifting it later in time by exactly one unit of time
Reflecting it about the vertical amplitude axis
Scaling its amplitude everywhere by a factor of two
correct_answer: Turning it into a causal signal that is zero for t < 0

question_text: For the sinusoid f(t) = A sin(2 pi f t + phi), the quantity omega = 2 pi f is called the:
options: Amplitude of the waveform
Start phase of the waveform in radians
Period of the waveform in seconds
Angular frequency in radians per second
correct_answer: Angular frequency in radians per second

question_text: Why does the course classify a pure sinusoid as a non-causal signal?
options: Its amplitude decays steadily toward zero as time increases
Being periodic, it has no start and no end in time
It is defined for negative values of time but not positive ones
It changes its frequency continuously as time goes on
correct_answer: Being periodic, it has no start and no end in time

question_text: For the real exponential f(t) = e^(alpha t), the sign of alpha determines that the signal is:
options: Growing when alpha < 0, and decaying when alpha > 0, for any real alpha
Periodic for each real value that alpha can happen to take on
Decaying when alpha < 0, constant when alpha = 0, and growing when alpha > 0
Constant at zero unless alpha happens to equal exactly one
correct_answer: Decaying when alpha < 0, constant when alpha = 0, and growing when alpha > 0

question_text: For a complex exponential with alpha = sigma + j omega, the real part sigma governs the envelope so that the signal is:
options: A pure sinusoid when sigma > 0, and a constant amplitude when sigma < 0
A constant-amplitude wave for each value that sigma may happen to take
A pure sinusoid when sigma = 0, growing when sigma > 0, and decaying (damped) when sigma < 0
A non-oscillatory signal for whatever value the frequency omega happens to take on
correct_answer: A pure sinusoid when sigma = 0, growing when sigma > 0, and decaying (damped) when sigma < 0

question_text: A gate (rectangular) signal of width tau can be written using unit step signals as:
options: The product of two shifted unit steps taken over the interval
The difference of two shifted unit steps, u(t + tau/2) - u(t - tau/2)
The integral of a single unit step evaluated over all of time
The derivative of a single unit step taken right at the origin
correct_answer: The difference of two shifted unit steps, u(t + tau/2) - u(t - tau/2)

question_text: Why is the unit impulse delta(t) described as a singularity (generalized) function rather than a regular function?
options: It takes a different finite constant value at each separate instant along the axis
It cannot be given an ordinary value even at t = 0 and is defined only through an integral
It stays non-zero over a wide but finite interval around the time origin
It is identical to the unit step function at each point along the time axis
correct_answer: It cannot be given an ordinary value even at t = 0 and is defined only through an integral

question_text: Starting from a gate signal of width tau and unit area, the unit impulse delta(t) is obtained by:
options: Shrinking the duration tau toward zero while keeping the area equal to one
Widening the duration tau while holding the pulse height fixed at one
Holding the duration fixed while raising the pulse height toward infinity
Averaging the gate signal over one full period of the waveform
correct_answer: Shrinking the duration tau toward zero while keeping the area equal to one

question_text: As the width tau of the unit-area gate shrinks toward zero, its amplitude:
options: Tends toward zero, so the impulse effectively vanishes from the signal
Tends toward infinity, so the impulse cannot be defined by a regular function
Stays fixed at one throughout the whole limiting process
Swings between plus one and minus one without ever settling down
correct_answer: Tends toward infinity, so the impulse cannot be defined by a regular function

question_text: The sampling (sifting) property of the impulse follows from the facts that delta(t) is zero for t not equal to 0 and that:
options: At t = 0 the other factor equals its value f(0), a constant, over the impulse
The impulse takes on a distinct value at each separate instant of time
The impulse integrates to a value of zero across the whole time axis
The impulse equals the unit step signal near the neighbourhood of the origin
correct_answer: At t = 0 the other factor equals its value f(0), a constant, over the impulse

question_text: When the impulse is scaled as A*delta(t), the constant A is referred to as the:
options: Angular frequency, equal to the rate of change of the impulse
Impulse intensity, equal to the area of the scaled impulse
Start phase, equal to the time offset applied to the impulse
Duration, equal to the width over which the impulse acts
correct_answer: Impulse intensity, equal to the area of the scaled impulse

question_text: The integral of the unit impulse delta(t) is:
options: Another impulse of twice the area
A decaying exponential signal
A constant equal to zero everywhere
The unit step signal
correct_answer: The unit step signal

question_text: With respect to symmetry, the unit impulse delta(t) is:
options: An odd function, so delta(t) = -delta(-t)
An even function, so delta(t) = delta(-t)
A causal function, zero for values of t below zero
A periodic function with some finite repetition period
correct_answer: An even function, so delta(t) = delta(-t)

question_text: The course shows that any signal f(t) can be represented as:
options: A single scaled copy of the unit step function of time
A product of two sinusoids lying at two different frequencies
A constant term plus one single decaying exponential term
A sum (limit of an integral) of shifted and weighted unit impulses
correct_answer: A sum (limit of an integral) of shifted and weighted unit impulses

question_text: In approximating f(t) by narrow rectangles, the rectangle at t = k*(delta-tau) is represented as f(k*delta-tau)*(delta-tau)*delta(t - k*delta-tau). Making delta-tau smaller:
options: Decreases the accuracy of the rectangle-based approximation
Increases the accuracy, becoming exact as delta-tau tends to d-tau
Leaves the accuracy of the approximation unchanged at each step
Removes the impulses entirely from the signal representation
correct_answer: Increases the accuracy, becoming exact as delta-tau tends to d-tau

question_text: A system is linear if, for scaling and additivity, it satisfies:
options: a*f1(t) + b*f2(t) produces a*y1(t) + b*y2(t)
f(t - t0) produces the shifted output y(t - t0) for any t0
The output equals the input multiplied by one fixed constant gain
f1(t)*f2(t) produces the product y1(t)*y2(t) for any two inputs
correct_answer: a*f1(t) + b*f2(t) produces a*y1(t) + b*y2(t)

question_text: A system is time-invariant if:
options: Shifting the input as f(t - t0) simply shifts the output to y(t - t0)
Scaling the input by a factor of a scales the output up to a*y(t)
Adding two separate inputs adds their two separate outputs
The output depends on the present value of the input alone
correct_answer: Shifting the input as f(t - t0) simply shifts the output to y(t - t0)

question_text: Why are linear time-invariant (LTI) systems so central to this analysis method?
options: Summing the responses to all the shifted, weighted impulses in f(t) works only for LTI systems
They form the sole class of systems capable of processing periodic input signals
They yield a valid output even without any known impulse response function being available
They convert each input signal into a single pure sinusoid at their output
correct_answer: Summing the responses to all the shifted, weighted impulses in f(t) works only for LTI systems

question_text: The response of an LTI system to the unit impulse delta(t) is given a special name and symbol:
options: The transfer function, denoted F(j*omega)
The unit step response, denoted u(t)
The unit impulse response, denoted h(t)
The system gain, denoted by the constant A
correct_answer: The unit impulse response, denoted h(t)

question_text: Why is the impulse response h(t) regarded as such an important descriptor of an LTI system?
options: Because it only gives the system response to a steady constant direct-current input
Because it fixes the system's operating frequency without needing any input
Because it lets you skip knowing the input signal when finding the output
Since any signal is a sum of shifted, weighted impulses, h(t) gives the response to any input
correct_answer: Since any signal is a sum of shifted, weighted impulses, h(t) gives the response to any input

question_text: When an input f(t) passes through an LTI system with impulse response h(t), the output is written y(t) = f(t) * h(t), where the operation "*" denotes:
options: Ordinary point-by-point multiplication
Convolution of f(t) and h(t)
Correlation of f(t) with itself
Simple addition of f(t) and h(t)
correct_answer: Convolution of f(t) and h(t)

question_text: Convolution y(t) = f(t) * h(t) is built from the elementary LTI facts that delta(t) -> h(t) and that:
options: A shifted impulse produces an unshifted, unscaled copy of h(t)
Any impulse produces the unit step response rather than h(t)
The impulse located at t = 0 alone produces a valid output
A shifted, scaled impulse a*delta(t - t0) produces a*h(t - t0)
correct_answer: A shifted, scaled impulse a*delta(t - t0) produces a*h(t - t0)

question_text: How does the course contrast the decomposition used in time-domain analysis with that used in frequency-domain analysis?
options: Time-domain uses shifted, weighted impulses; frequency-domain uses a sinusoid plus harmonics
Both of the approaches decompose the signal into shifted, weighted impulses in time
Time-domain analysis uses sinusoids and harmonics while frequency-domain uses impulses
Neither of the approaches decomposes the signal; each processes it as a single whole
correct_answer: Time-domain uses shifted, weighted impulses; frequency-domain uses a sinusoid plus harmonics

question_text: The Fourier series is a tool that applies specifically to:
options: Causal signals
Non-periodic signals
Periodic signals
Impulse signals
correct_answer: Periodic signals

question_text: In frequency-domain analysis, a signal is decomposed into:
options: A set of shifted and weighted impulse functions
A single decaying exponential component in time
A product of two unit step functions of time
A fundamental sinusoid together with its harmonics
correct_answer: A fundamental sinusoid together with its harmonics

question_text: The sampling function that arises in the spectrum of a periodic rectangular waveform is:
options: Sa(x) = sin(x)/x
Sa(x) = cos(x)/x
Sa(x) = x*sin(x)
correct_answer: Sa(x) = sin(x)/x

question_text: The Fourier transform is introduced as the tool needed when a signal is:
options: Periodic, though repeating only over a very short period of time
Constant in both its time variable and its amplitude value
Non-periodic, formed as a periodic signal's period tends to infinity
Defined at only a single isolated instant along the time axis
correct_answer: Non-periodic, formed as a periodic signal's period tends to infinity

question_text: As the period T of a periodic signal is expanded toward infinity, both the line amplitude Fn and the spacing omega_0 tend to zero, which motivates:
options: Keeping the discrete frequency lines exactly as they were
Discarding all of the frequency information about the signal
Introducing spectrum density instead of discrete frequency lines
Treating the whole signal as a single impulse located in time
correct_answer: Introducing spectrum density instead of discrete frequency lines

question_text: The Fourier transform of a unit impulse delta(t) is a constant across all frequencies, which means the impulse:
options: Contains only one single frequency component in its spectrum
Has uniform frequency density and therefore an infinitely wide band
Has essentially no frequency content anywhere in its spectrum
Is band-limited to a narrow range of low frequencies
correct_answer: Has uniform frequency density and therefore an infinitely wide band

question_text: The Fourier transform of a constant (DC) signal of value 1 is:
options: A constant density spread across all frequencies
An impulse at zero frequency, 2*pi*delta(omega)
A pair of impulses at plus and minus omega_0
A sinc-shaped spectrum centred at the origin
correct_answer: An impulse at zero frequency, 2*pi*delta(omega)

question_text: Why does the spectrum of the constant signal 1 consist of an impulse only at omega = 0?
options: A constant represents a direct-current signal, whose energy lies entirely at zero frequency
A constant carries equal amounts of energy at every single frequency that is present
A constant is a high-frequency signal that occupies only a very narrow band
A constant places its energy at a pair of separate carrier frequencies only
correct_answer: A constant represents a direct-current signal, whose energy lies entirely at zero frequency

question_text: The Fourier transform of cos(omega_0 t) consists of:
options: A single impulse located exactly at zero frequency
A uniform density spread across all of the frequencies
A pair of impulses located at plus and minus omega_0
A sinc-shaped lobe centred at omega_0 by itself
correct_answer: A pair of impulses located at plus and minus omega_0

question_text: The linearity property of the Fourier transform states that:
options: The transform of a product equals the product of the two transforms
The transform of a sum equals the larger of the two transforms
Scaling a signal in time has no effect at all on its transform
The transform of a*f1(t) + b*f2(t) is a*F1(j*omega) + b*F2(j*omega)
correct_answer: The transform of a*f1(t) + b*f2(t) is a*F1(j*omega) + b*F2(j*omega)

question_text: According to the time-shift property, delaying a signal by t0 in the time domain corresponds in the frequency domain to:
options: Scaling the magnitude of the whole spectrum by the delay value of t0
Sliding the entire spectrum bodily along the frequency axis by t0 units
Adding a fixed constant phase equal to t0 radians at each frequency
Multiplying the spectrum by the phase e^(-j*omega*t0), the magnitude unchanged
correct_answer: Multiplying the spectrum by the phase e^(-j*omega*t0), the magnitude unchanged

question_text: The frequency-shift (modulation) property says that multiplying f(t) by e^(j*omega_0 t) in the time domain:
options: Multiplies the spectrum by the constant factor e^(-j*omega_0)
Delays the signal by omega_0 seconds along the time axis
Shifts the spectrum to F[j(omega - omega_0)] in the frequency domain
Leaves the spectrum of the signal unaffected altogether
correct_answer: Shifts the spectrum to F[j(omega - omega_0)] in the frequency domain

question_text: Multiplying a baseband signal f(t) by a carrier cos(omega_0 t) produces a spectrum that is:
options: A single copy of F(j*omega) left sitting right at the frequency origin
An impulse at zero frequency scaled by the carrier amplitude
The original spectrum F(j*omega) with its bandwidth halved
Two half-amplitude copies of F(j*omega) centred at plus and minus omega_0
correct_answer: Two half-amplitude copies of F(j*omega) centred at plus and minus omega_0

question_text: Parseval's relation (the energy theorem) expresses that:
options: The total energy of a real-valued signal always works out to be zero
The phase of a signal carries the whole of its energy information
Energy is conserved only for perfectly periodic signals but not for others
The total energy of a signal can be computed in the time or the frequency domain
correct_answer: The total energy of a signal can be computed in the time or the frequency domain

question_text: The quantity |F(j*omega)|^2 is called the signal's energy spectrum because it represents:
options: The instantaneous power carried by the signal at each separate moment in time
The phase of the signal expressed as a function of the frequency
The signal energy contained in a unit band of frequency, carrying no phase information
The total count of the frequency lines making up the whole spectrum
correct_answer: The signal energy contained in a unit band of frequency, carrying no phase information

question_text: The time-domain convolution theorem of the Fourier transform states that:
options: Convolution in time corresponds instead to convolution of the two spectra as well
Convolution in time corresponds to simple addition of the two spectra
Convolution in time leaves each of the two signal spectra unchanged
Convolution in time corresponds to multiplication of the spectra, F1(j*omega)*F2(j*omega)
correct_answer: Convolution in time corresponds to multiplication of the spectra, F1(j*omega)*F2(j*omega)

question_text: The frequency-domain convolution theorem states that multiplication of two signals in time corresponds in frequency to:
options: Convolution of their spectra, scaled by a factor of 1/(2*pi)
Multiplication of their spectra with no extra scaling factor
Addition of their two spectra with a factor of 2*pi applied
The difference of their two spectra taken across frequency
correct_answer: Convolution of their spectra, scaled by a factor of 1/(2*pi)

question_text: What broad usefulness does the convolution theorem provide, according to the slides?
options: It converts an input signal into a single sharp impulse located firmly in time
It removes the need to know a system's impulse response when solving
It applies solely to signals that happen to be perfectly periodic ones
It turns convolution in one domain into an algebraic operation in the other domain
correct_answer: It turns convolution in one domain into an algebraic operation in the other domain

question_text: For a linear system, the quantity H(j*omega) that relates input and output spectra is called the:
options: Energy spectrum of the applied input signal in frequency
Impulse intensity of the system
System function, also called the transfer function
Sampling function of the output
correct_answer: System function, also called the transfer function

question_text: If a system has impulse response h(t) and transfer function H(j*omega), then the output spectrum is given by:
options: Y(j*omega) = F(j*omega)*H(j*omega), the product of input spectrum and transfer function
Y(j*omega) = F(j*omega) + H(j*omega), the sum of the input and the function
Y(j*omega) = F(j*omega) / H(j*omega), the ratio of the input to the transfer function
Y(j*omega) = F(j*omega), taken independently of the system's own function
correct_answer: Y(j*omega) = F(j*omega)*H(j*omega), the product of input spectrum and transfer function

question_text: The fact that Y(j*omega) = F(j*omega)*H(j*omega) in the frequency domain corresponds in the time domain to:
options: The product y(t) = f(t)*h(t) taken sample by sample in time
The sum y(t) = f(t) + h(t) taken point by point in time
The convolution y(t) = f(t) * h(t) taken in the time domain
The derivative of f(t) with respect to time at each instant
correct_answer: The convolution y(t) = f(t) * h(t) taken in the time domain

question_text: If a system is too complicated to express analytically, the slides suggest measuring its transfer function by:
options: Applying sine inputs at different frequencies, measuring each output, and combining them
Applying a single impulse and reading off the final steady-state value
Applying a constant direct-current input and then scaling up the measured result
Computing the ratio between two arbitrarily chosen samples in time
correct_answer: Applying sine inputs at different frequencies, measuring each output, and combining them

question_text: The technique of driving a system with sine inputs across a range of frequencies to characterise it is called:
options: A convolution sum
A frequency sweep
A time reversal
An impulse decomposition
correct_answer: A frequency sweep

question_text: Euler's relation is invoked in this material chiefly to:
options: Express sine and cosine signals in terms of complex exponentials
Convert a periodic signal into an equivalent causal signal
Prove that the unit impulse is an even function of time
Define the sampling interval used for a discrete signal
correct_answer: Express sine and cosine signals in terms of complex exponentials

question_text: The Fourier transform of the one-sided exponential e^(-a t)*u(t) with a > 0 has a magnitude spectrum that:
options: Is a pair of sharp impulses located at plus and minus a
Is flat and equal in value at every one of the frequencies
Is zero at the low frequencies and then rises without any upper bound
Is largest at zero frequency and then rolls off as the frequency increases
correct_answer: Is largest at zero frequency and then rolls off as the frequency increases

question_text: In the time domain, a discrete-time signal is represented as:
options: A continuous waveform defined at every instant
A single scalar value that never changes in time
A frequency spectrum holding no time information
A sequence of numbers, called samples
correct_answer: A sequence of numbers, called samples

question_text: When a discrete-time sequence is formed by sampling a continuous signal x_a(t), the n-th sample is given by:
options: x[n] = x_a(t) integrated from time 0 up to t = nT
x[n] = x_a(nT), the value of x_a(t) taken at t = nT
x[n] = x_a(t) averaged across the interval of width T
x[n] = the derivative of x_a(t) evaluated at t = nT
correct_answer: x[n] = x_a(nT), the value of x_a(t) taken at t = nT

question_text: The spacing T between two consecutive samples is called the sampling interval, and its reciprocal 1/T is called the:
options: Angular frequency of the samples
Fundamental period of the sequence
Quantization step of the sequence
Sampling frequency
correct_answer: Sampling frequency

question_text: The course distinguishes sampled-data signals from digital signals by noting that:
options: Sampled-data signals have continuous-valued samples, while digital signals have discrete-valued samples
Sampled-data signals have discrete-valued samples, while the digital ones are continuous-valued
Both sampled-data and digital signals turn out to have continuous-valued samples
Sampled-data signals alone are the ones actually defined at discrete time instants
correct_answer: Sampled-data signals have continuous-valued samples, while digital signals have discrete-valued samples

question_text: Signals in a practical DSP system are digital signals, obtained from sample values by:
options: Convolving them with the unit step sequence in time
Quantizing them, either by rounding or by truncation
Reversing them in time about the sampling origin
Interpolating them up to a higher sampling rate
correct_answer: Quantizing them, either by rounding or by truncation

question_text: A right-sided sequence has zero-valued samples for n < N1. It is additionally called a causal sequence when:
options: N1 is a non-integer value
N1 tends to negative infinity

question_text: In the modulation (product) operation on sequences, the output is formed by:
options: Adding the two input sequences sample by sample, y[n] = x[n] + w[n]
Delaying one of the input sequences by a single sampling interval
Multiplying the two input sequences sample by sample, y[n] = x[n]*w[n]
Reversing one input sequence in time before they are combined
correct_answer: Multiplying the two input sequences sample by sample, y[n] = x[n]*w[n]

question_text: The scalar-multiplication operation on a sequence produces:
options: y[n] = A*x[n], each sample scaled by a constant A
y[n] = x[n] + A, a constant A added to each sample
y[n] = x[n - A], the sequence delayed by A samples
y[n] = x[A*n], the sequence resampled in the time index
correct_answer: y[n] = A*x[n], each sample scaled by a constant A

question_text: A unit-delay operation applied to x[n] produces the output:
options: y[n] = x[-n]
y[n] = A*x[n]

question_text: The time-reversal (folding) operation on a sequence produces:
options: y[n] = x[n] + x[-n]
y[n] = x[-n]
y[n] = x[n]*x[-n]
correct_answer: y[n] = x[-n]

question_text: The branching operation in a discrete-time structure is used to:
options: Combine several separate sequences into just one single output
Delay a sequence by exactly one sampling period in time
Provide multiple copies of a sequence for use at different points
Reverse a sequence about the origin of the time axis
correct_answer: Provide multiple copies of a sequence for use at different points

question_text: In sampling-rate alteration, the ratio R = F'_T / F_T describes the change of rate. The process is called interpolation when:
options: R < 1, giving a lower sampling rate
R = 1, leaving the rate unchanged
R is negative, reversing the sequence
R > 1, giving a higher sampling rate
correct_answer: R > 1, giving a higher sampling rate

question_text: In sampling-rate alteration, the process is called decimation when:
options: R > 1, giving a higher sampling rate
R = 0, removing all of the samples
R < 1, giving a lower sampling rate
R = 1, leaving the rate unchanged
correct_answer: R < 1, giving a lower sampling rate

question_text: A discrete-time sequence is classified as periodic when:
options: Its samples all settle to one and the same constant value
It has only a finite number of non-zero samples in total
Its samples decay steadily toward zero as n increases
It repeats, so that x[n] equals x[n + N] for some period N
correct_answer: It repeats, so that x[n] equals x[n + N] for some period N

question_text: With respect to length and energy, which statement matches the course's classification?
options: A finite-length sequence with finite sample values instead has infinite energy
An infinite-length sequence is guaranteed to end up with finite energy
A sequence that has finite energy is bound to have an infinite length
A finite-length sequence with finite sample values always has finite energy
correct_answer: A finite-length sequence with finite sample values always has finite energy

question_text: A sequence is classified as a power signal when it has:
options: Infinite energy but finite average power, as a periodic sequence has
Finite energy but zero average power, as a short sequence has
Both finite energy and finite average power at the same time
Zero energy together with zero average power everywhere
correct_answer: Infinite energy but finite average power, as a periodic sequence has

question_text: A sequence is classified as an energy signal when it has:
options: Infinite energy but finite average power, as a periodic sequence has
Infinite energy together with an infinite average power at once
Finite energy together with a finite, non-zero average power
Finite energy but zero average power, as a finite-length sequence has
correct_answer: Finite energy but zero average power, as a finite-length sequence has

question_text: A sequence x[n] is said to be bounded when:
options: Its magnitude stays below a finite limit for all n, as cos(0.3*pi*n) does
The sum of all of its sample values turns out to be finite
The sum of the squares of all of its sample values turns out finite
It has only a finite number of non-zero samples in total
correct_answer: Its magnitude stays below a finite limit for all n, as cos(0.3*pi*n) does

question_text: The two fundamental basic sequences introduced first in the discrete-time material are:
options: The gate sequence and the linear ramp sequence
The chirp sequence and the constant sequence
The random sequence and the periodic sequence
The unit sample sequence and the unit step sequence
correct_answer: The unit sample sequence and the unit step sequence

question_text: A real sinusoidal sequence is written x[n] = A*cos(omega_0*n + phi), where the symbol omega_0 is the:
options: Angular frequency of the sequence
Amplitude of the sequence
Phase offset of the sequence
Sampling interval of the sequence
correct_answer: Angular frequency of the sequence

question_text: For a complex exponential sequence, the real part sigma_0 of the exponent controls the amplitude so that the real sinusoidal parts are:
options: Constant when sigma_0 = 0, growing when sigma_0 > 0, and decaying when sigma_0 < 0
Constant when sigma_0 > 0, and growing when sigma_0 turns out to equal zero
Growing whenever sigma_0 is less than zero, for any amplitude
Held at zero unless sigma_0 turns out to equal exactly one
correct_answer: Constant when sigma_0 = 0, growing when sigma_0 > 0, and decaying when sigma_0 < 0

question_text: A sinusoidal sequence A*cos(omega_0*n + phi) is periodic only when:
options: omega_0 is any real number that is greater than zero
omega_0 equals the sampling frequency of the sequence exactly
omega_0*N = 2*pi*r for positive integers N and r
N is chosen freely as any convenient non-integer value
correct_answer: omega_0*N = 2*pi*r for positive integers N and r

question_text: For a periodic sequence, the fundamental period N is:
options: The largest value of N that satisfies the periodicity condition
The smallest value of N satisfying omega_0*N = 2*pi*r
Any value of N for which omega_0*N is a whole integer
A value equal to the amplitude A of the sinusoidal sequence
correct_answer: The smallest value of N satisfying omega_0*N = 2*pi*r

question_text: The sampling theorem (Nyquist theorem) states that a continuous signal can be represented uniquely by its samples if the sampling frequency is:
options: Equal to the highest frequency that is contained in the signal
Less than half of the highest frequency present in the signal
Set independently of which frequencies are present in the signal
Greater than twice the highest frequency contained in the signal
correct_answer: Greater than twice the highest frequency contained in the signal

question_text: The specific problem that the sampling theorem is meant to prevent is:
options: Quantization error, which grows when too few bits are used
Truncation, which cuts the sequence down to a finite length
Phase loss, which discards the timing detail of the signal
Aliasing, which occurs when the sampling frequency is too low
correct_answer: Aliasing, which occurs when the sampling frequency is too low

question_text: A discrete-time system is defined to be linear when, for x[n] = a*x1[n] + b*x2[n], the output is:
options: y[n] = y1[n - n0], a shifted version of one of the responses
y[n] = y1[n]*y2[n], the product of the two responses formed
y[n] = a*y1[n] + b*y2[n] for any constants a and b and any inputs
y[n] = a*y1[n] on its own, disregarding the second input
correct_answer: y[n] = a*y1[n] + b*y2[n] for any constants a and b and any inputs

question_text: A discrete-time system is shift-invariant when a shift of the input by n0, so that x[n] = x1[n - n0], produces:
options: y[n] = y1[n - n0], the same response shifted along by n0
y[n] = y1[n], the same response with no shift applied to it
y[n] = n0*y1[n], the response scaled by the factor n0
y[n] = y1[-n], the response reversed about the time origin
correct_answer: y[n] = y1[n - n0], the same response shifted along by n0

question_text: A linear time-invariant (LTI) discrete-time system is one that:
options: Satisfies linearity but fails the shift-invariance property
Satisfies shift-invariance but fails the linearity property
Satisfies both the linearity and the shift-invariance properties
Satisfies neither property yet remains causal in all cases
correct_answer: Satisfies both the linearity and the shift-invariance properties

question_text: Why are LTI discrete-time systems emphasised so strongly in the course?
options: They form the sole class that is able to process periodic input sequences properly
They produce an output without any impulse response being known
They require the sampling rate to be altered before they are used
They are easy to analyze, characterize and design, and support many useful algorithms
correct_answer: They are easy to analyze, characterize and design, and support many useful algorithms

question_text: The response of a discrete-time system to a unit sample sequence delta[n] is called the:
options: Unit impulse response, denoted h[n]
Unit step response, denoted s[n]
Transfer function, denoted by H
Convolution sum, denoted y[n]
correct_answer: Unit impulse response, denoted h[n]

question_text: A key consequence of the linear, time-invariant property is that an LTI discrete-time system is:
options: Characterized instead by its unit step response
Independent of whatever input is applied to it
Fully described by a single output sample value
Completely characterized by its impulse response
correct_answer: Completely characterized by its impulse response

question_text: Because any input can be written as a linear combination of shifted unit samples, the response of an LTI system to an input x[k]*delta[n - k] is:
options: x[k]*delta[n - k], left unchanged by the system
x[k]*h[n - k]
h[n], taken independently of the index k
x[n]*h[k], with the two indices swapped over
correct_answer: x[k]*h[n - k]

question_text: The summation that combines x[n] and h[n] to give the output of an LTI system, written y[n] = x[n] * h[n], is called the:
options: Fourier series
Convolution sum
Frequency sweep
Sampling sum
correct_answer: Convolution sum

question_text: The commutative property of the convolution sum states that:
options: x[n] * h[n] = x[n] + h[n]
x[n] * h[n] varies with the operand order
x[n] * h[n] = h[n] * x[n]
correct_answer: x[n] * h[n] = h[n] * x[n]

question_text: The distributive property of the convolution sum states that:
options: x[n] * (h[n] + y[n]) = x[n] * h[n] on its own
x[n] * (h[n] + y[n]) = h[n] + y[n] regardless of x

question_text: In the graphical interpretation of the convolution sum, the impulse response h[k] is first:
options: Scaled by a fixed constant, then integrated over all of the values of k
Left just as it is, then added straight onto the sequence x[k]
Time-reversed to form h[-k], then shifted before multiplying and summing
Resampled to a higher rate, then quantized before being summed
correct_answer: Time-reversed to form h[-k], then shifted before multiplying and summing

question_text: If two sequences of lengths M and N are convolved, the resulting sequence has length:
options: M + N
M + N - 1
M * N
the larger of M and N
correct_answer: M + N - 1

question_text: A discrete-time LTI system is classified as a finite impulse response (FIR) system when its impulse response h[n] is:
options: Of infinite length
Of finite length
Equal to the unit step sequence
Undefined for negative values of n
correct_answer: Of finite length

question_text: A discrete-time LTI system is classified as an infinite impulse response (IIR) system when its impulse response is:
options: Of finite length
Zero outside one single sample
Of infinite length
Identical to its own input sequence
correct_answer: Of infinite length

question_text: The IIR systems studied in this course are characterized mathematically by:
options: Finite sums of products with no feedback path
Linear constant-coefficient difference equations
A single scalar-multiplication operation
The Fourier series of a periodic signal
correct_answer: Linear constant-coefficient difference equations

question_text: The discrete-time accumulator defined by y[n] = y[n - 1] + x[n] is given as an example of:
options: An FIR system, since it uses present and past inputs only
A non-linear system, since it adds two signals together
An IIR system, since its impulse response is of infinite length
A time-varying system, since its coefficients change over time
correct_answer: An IIR system, since its impulse response is of infinite length

question_text: A discrete-time system is called non-recursive when its output can be computed:
options: Using past output samples along with the inputs
Without knowing any of the input samples at all
From just the present and past input samples
Once the whole input sequence has been received
correct_answer: From just the present and past input samples

question_text: A discrete-time system is called recursive when its output computation:
options: Uses just the single present input sample each time
Uses present and past input samples but no outputs
Involves past output samples besides present and past inputs
Leaves out all the earlier values of the input and the output
correct_answer: Involves past output samples besides present and past inputs

question_text: The response of a discrete-time system to a unit step sequence is called the:
options: Unit impulse response, denoted h[n]
Convolution sum, denoted y[n]
Transfer function, denoted H[n]
Unit step response, denoted s[n]
correct_answer: Unit step response, denoted s[n]

question_text: An arbitrary discrete-time sequence can be represented in the time domain as:
options: A single scaled copy of the unit step sequence in time
The product of two sinusoidal sequences of different rates
A weighted sum of a basic sequence and its shifted versions
A constant term plus one single decaying exponential term
correct_answer: A weighted sum of a basic sequence and its shifted versions

question_text: For a complex exponential sequence written A*alpha^n, the symbols A and alpha are, in general:
options: Strictly positive integers
Real or complex numbers
Numbers equal to one another
Values between zero and one
correct_answer: Real or complex numbers
